paragraphs: Algebra is arithmetic with a gap left in it. You write a letter where an unknown number goes and reason about it. People study it because one short line with a letter in it describes every case of something at once: the fare for a taxi trip of any length, or the amount left in a savings pot after any number of months. It is also the shorthand used in science and computing, which makes it hard to read much further in either without it.

The course has six lessons in two parts. The first three, called Rearranging, teach you to read a letter as a number you haven't been told yet, then to find that number by doing the same thing to both sides of an equation and undoing one step at a time. The last three, called Straight lines, put numbers on a grid and measure how steep a line is. The final lesson links a line on the page to the equation that draws it.
Each lesson explains first and asks afterwards, so you meet a question only once you have been shown what it needs.
outcomes: You'll be able to read an expression such as 3x − 4 as a calculation and work out its value for any number.
You'll be able to solve an equation such as 3x + 2 = 23 and say why each step keeps it true.
You'll be able to undo a calculation in the right order, including one with brackets.
You'll be able to find the gradient of a straight line from two points on it.
You'll be able to draw the line for y = mx + c and read its equation back off the line.
prerequisites: You should be comfortable with whole-number arithmetic, which is all the course assumes.
